lessons.title: Fire procedures and types of fire
lessons.html:
Fire on the farm

Fires on farms start in workshops, sheds with hay and fuel, kitchens and houses, electrical boxes, and in the veld. A veld fire in dry winter in Mpumalanga or the Free State can spread for kilometres and kill people and livestock. Every worker must know what to do.

The fire triangle

A fire needs three things: fuel (something to burn), heat and oxygen (air). Take away one and the fire goes out. Water removes heat, a fire blanket or foam removes oxygen, and a firebreak removes fuel.

Workplace fire procedure

  1. Raise the alarm: shout "Fire!", use the siren or bell, and phone the emergency number on your farm's list.
  2. Make people safe: get people out of danger; help those who need it.
  3. Decide: is the fire small and can you fight it safely, with a way out behind you? If not, leave.
  4. Fight only if trained and safe.
  5. Evacuate to the assembly point. Do not go back for belongings.
  6. Report to the person in charge.

Classes of fire

ClassFuelFarm example
AOrdinary solids: wood, paper, grass, straw, clothHay bale, veld grass, pallets
BFlammable liquids: petrol, diesel, oil, paint, solventsFuel spill at the diesel tank
CFlammable gases: LPG, acetyleneGas bottle in the kitchen or workshop
DBurning metalsRare on farms
FCooking oils and fatsPot of oil in the kitchen

Fires involving electrical equipment (switch boxes, motors, wiring) need special care: never use water on live electrical equipment. Switch off the power at the main switch if it is safe to do so.

Know the context too: is there fuel, gas or chemicals nearby that could explode? Is the fire spreading towards a building or crops? This decides whether you fight or leave.

lessons.title: Fire fighting equipment and how to use it
lessons.html:
Choose the right equipment

EquipmentUse onDo not use on
Water (hose reel, water extinguisher, knapsack)Class AElectrical, oil, fuel, cooking oil
Dry chemical powder (DCP)Classes A, B, C and electricalCan be messy; powder reduces visibility
Carbon dioxide (CO2)Class B and electricalLittle effect outdoors in wind; do not touch the horn, it gets freezing cold
FoamClasses A and BLive electrical equipment
Fire blanketSmall pan fires, clothing on fireLarge fires
Fire beatersSmall veld firesLarge fast fires

Always read the label on the extinguisher. Never throw water on burning cooking oil; it explodes into a fireball. Smother it with a fire blanket or a lid and switch off the heat.

Checking equipment

  • Extinguisher is in its place, visible and not blocked.
  • Safety pin and seal are in place.
  • Pressure gauge needle is in the green.
  • Service tag shows it is in date.
  • No damage to the hose or body.
  • Hose reels: hose not cracked, water on.

Report missing, used or damaged equipment at once so it can be replaced.

Safety equipment for you

For veld fires: cotton or fire-resistant clothing (not nylon, which melts), boots, gloves, goggles and a hat. Carry water to drink.

Using an extinguisher: PASS

  1. Pull the pin.
  2. Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, not the flames.
  3. Squeeze the handle.
  4. Sweep from side to side across the base.

Stand a few metres back, with the wind behind you outdoors and your exit behind you indoors. Move closer as the fire gets smaller. Watch for re-ignition.

lessons.title: Fighting the fire, retreating and reporting
lessons.html:
Fighting a containable fire

A containable fire is small, not spreading fast, and you can fight it with the equipment at hand while keeping a safe way out. Examples: a small rubbish fire, a burning tyre, a small pan fire, a small fire on a bale.

  • Never fight a fire alone if you can avoid it. One person fights; another brings more equipment or calls for help.
  • Keep low to avoid smoke and heat. Smoke kills more people than flames.
  • Keep your exit behind you. Never let the fire get between you and the way out.
  • Use one extinguisher; if the fire is not clearly going out, use a second only if it is still safe.
  • For a veld fire, attack from the burnt side, working with the team on the flanks. Use beaters to smother the edge. Never stand in front of a running fire or in tall grass downwind of it.

When to retreat

Leave immediately if:

  • The fire is getting bigger or spreading to other materials.
  • Your extinguisher is empty and the fire is still burning.
  • Smoke is filling the room or you struggle to breathe.
  • Gas bottles, fuel tanks or chemicals are close to the fire.
  • The wind changes direction in a veld fire.

Back away facing the fire, close doors behind you to slow it, and go to the assembly point. Hand over to the fire brigade, the farm's fire team or the fire protection association. Tell them: what is burning, where, if anyone is missing, and where gas, fuel or chemicals are.

After the fire

  • Keep watching for flare-ups. Smouldering bales and stumps can reignite hours later.
  • Report the fire on the incident form: date, time, place, cause if known, what was used to fight it, injuries and damage.
  • Report every extinguisher you used, even partly. A used extinguisher must be refilled or replaced; never hang it back on the wall.

Key points

  • Raise the alarm first, then decide whether it is safe to fight.
  • Match the extinguisher to the class of fire; no water on electrical, fuel or cooking oil fires.
  • Use PASS and aim at the base of the fire.
  • Keep your exit behind you and retreat if the fire grows.
  • Report the fire and every extinguisher used.
